paragraphs: Tebila zo hi mishshum pelitat tuma kede sheyyetze hakkeli mittumato liqdushshat yisrael duvmya deger sheyyatza mereshut haakku"m lirshut yisrael hilkak apillu hem chadashim shelleqachan min haumman goy tzarik lehatbilam vaapillu lehishtammesh bo tzonen asur belo tebila veim yisrael sakar o shaal keli min haggoy en tzarik tebila vedavqa kele seuda tzerikin tebila mishshum dehakkatub ayre bikle seuda diktib kol asher yabo baesh veku' veezehu dabar shebba baesh vetzarik lehakshiro baesh heve omer zeh keli seuda shebbolea "y haesh shetztzarik lehaplit baleu "y haesh:

clarification.explanation: Immersing vessels is meant to remove from them the "impurity" of gentile ownership, so the vessel passes from the gentile's domain into "Israel's sanctity" — similar to a convert who leaves the domain of the gentiles and enters Israel's domain. For this reason even entirely new vessels, bought directly from a gentile craftsman, require immersion, and even to use them cold (with no heat) without cooking — it is forbidden without immersion. But if a Jew only rented or borrowed a vessel from a gentile (did not buy it), no immersion is needed, since the vessel did not truly transfer into Jewish ownership. Immersion is required specifically for meal vessels (vessels used for eating and cooking), since the verse speaks of a vessel "that comes through fire" — that is, a vessel normally koshered by fire (since it absorbs through fire and must expel what it absorbed).
takeaways: Vessel immersion is required for meal vessels bought from a gentile (even new ones), to remove them from "gentile ownership" — even for cold use, immersion is required.
A vessel merely borrowed or rented from a gentile (not bought) requires no immersion, since it did not transfer to Jewish ownership.

paragraphs: Apillu kele seuda enam tzerikin tebila min hattora ella raq kele mattakot diktib zahab vekesep abal kele cheres ukele etz veeben en tzerikin tebila veamenam chaza"l tiqqenu tebila likle zekukit mippene shehen domin qetzat likle barzel yaan deim nishtabberu yesh lahem taqqana sheyyekolim lehattikan velaasot mehem keli acher ulehaki tzerikin tebila midderabbanan veyesh omerim degam kele mattakot tebilatan midderabbanan uqera asmakta bealema vesabera rishona iqqar disbira lah kele mattakot middeorayta veayyen peri chadash uperi toar veerek hashshulchan ushear acharonim:

clarification.explanation: Even among meal vessels, only metal vessels are Torah-obligated in immersion (since the verse mentions gold and silver), but earthenware, wood, and stone vessels require no immersion at all by Torah law. Nevertheless, the Sages instituted immersion also for glass vessels, since they are in some measure similar to metal vessels — since if broken, they can be re-melted and made into another vessel, and their immersion is therefore rabbinic. There is an opinion that even metal vessels themselves are obligated in immersion only rabbinically, and the verse is merely a supporting text (a mere hint), but the primary view is that metal vessels are Torah-obligated in immersion.
takeaways: By Torah law, only metal vessels (gold and silver) are obligated in immersion; earthenware, wood, and stone are exempt.
Glass vessels are rabbinically obligated, since they resemble metal vessels (able to be re-melted).

paragraphs: Tzarik lehatbil kol hakkeli sheyyakniso kullo bemayim velo yishshaer mimmennu chutz lammayim apillu kol shehu veim hu gadol veeno yakol lehatbilo kullo bepaam achat katab harab chakemat adam za"l kelal "g ot t"v deasur lehatbilo lachatzain sheyyatbil techilla tzad echad veyachazor veyatbil tzad hashsheni debaenan kan duvmya ditbilat hannidda shetztzarik shettihyeh kullah bemayim bepaam achat sheen zeh domeh lehagala dehatam hu magil lehaplit haissur vekevan dehigil cheleq echad mimmennu palat haissur meoto hacheleq velaken chozer umagil cheleq hannishar abal haka hu mishshum tuma vekevan demiqtzato chutz lammayim tachazor hattuma vetitpashshet bekol hakkeli ayyen sham venirim debarayv vetzarik lehizzaher bazeh:

clarification.explanation: The entire vessel must be immersed so that it is all in the water at once, with no part remaining outside the water — even a minute amount. If the vessel is too large to immerse it all at once, it is forbidden to immerse it in halves (one side first, then the other), since vessel immersion resembles a niddah's immersion, which must be entirely in the water at once. This differs from purging, where each part purged expels its own absorbed prohibition separately, and one may purge part after part. But immersion concerns removing impurity, and as long as part of the vessel remains outside the water, the impurity returns and spreads throughout the whole vessel.
takeaways: The entire vessel must be immersed at once, with no part remaining outside the water; a large vessel may not be immersed in halves (unlike purging, which may be done part by part).

paragraphs: Ben kele mattakot ben kele zekukit beet shemmatbilam yebarek qodem tebila qb"v al tebilat kelim veim matbil keli echad bilbad yebarek al tebilat kele ubediabad im berak al keli echad tebilat kelim yatza dimpareshinan milleteh al kelim dealema qae vehu haddin lehepek name yatza veayyen peri chadash vetzarik lehatbil gam yedot hakkelim vetob lomar qodem habberaka pasuq vayhi noam veku'.

clarification.explanation: For both metal and glass vessels, before immersion one blesses "who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding the immersion of vessels." If immersing only one vessel, one blesses "regarding the immersion of a vessel" (singular). After the fact, even if one blessed in the plural ("immersion of vessels") over one vessel, or conversely in the singular ("immersion of a vessel") over several vessels, one has fulfilled the obligation, since the intent is correctly understood either way. One must also immerse the vessels' handles (not only the body of the vessel). It is good to say the verse "Vihi Noam" before the blessing.
takeaways: One blesses "regarding the immersion of vessels" (or the singular "vessel") before immersing — after the fact, either wording suffices.
The handles must also be immersed, and it is good to say "Vihi Noam" before the blessing.

paragraphs: Kelim ellu shetztzerikin tebila apillu en shotin bahem veen mebashshelim bahem ella maknisin bahem yayin leqiyyum kegon tzelochiyyot gedolot sheqqorin bearbe qrry"b (mikele zekukit gedolim lenozelim) tzarik lebarek al tebilatam ukemo shekkatab harab bet david za"l siman s"b veap al gab deharab bet yeuddeh siman n"b choleq haiqqar keharab bet david za"l veayyen lehaggaon chida" za"l beshiyyure beraka shehebi dibre bet david za"l vekatab vehebi reayot lidbarayv ayyen sham limmed bemillot qetzarot ellu detamo venimmuqo immo veken hamminhag poh irenu bagdad y" yaan ki hrh"g mv"r zeqeni rabbenu mosheh chayyim zlh"h kak haya doresh bekol shana bashshabbat haggadol veken nahag acharayv ateret rashe adoni abi zlh"h bidrush shabbat haggadol veken nahagti ana abeda lehorot ken bidrush shabbat haggadol bs"d.

clarification.explanation: Even vessels not used for drinking or cooking, but only for storage (such as large flasks for storing wine), require immersion with a blessing — as Rabbi "Beit David" wrote. Some disagree (Rabbi "Beit Yehuda"), but the halacha is ruled following "Beit David," and so was the practice of the Ben Ish Chai himself and his ancestors, who taught this every year on the Great Sabbath, and so is also the Baghdad custom.
takeaways: Vessels used only for storage (not drinking/cooking) are also obligated in immersion with a blessing, following "Beit David"'s view, ruled and practiced in Baghdad.

paragraphs: Gam kelim shel blv"r (qerisetal) tzerikin beraka kemo zekukit sheqqorin gaziz (zekukit regila) yaan ki byrvp" mattikin et kol min hblv"r kemo zekukit veosin oto kelim chadashim beopen deen min blv"r baolam shello yattiku oto kizkukit lekak dino kizkukit mammash shetztzarik tebila bibraka:

clarification.explanation: Crystal vessels require immersion with a blessing exactly like ordinary glass vessels, since in Europe all types of crystal are melted exactly like ordinary glass and made into new vessels — there is no crystal that cannot be melted like glass, and its law is therefore exactly that of glass.
takeaways: Crystal vessels have exactly the law of glass (able to be re-melted like it) — obligated in immersion with a blessing.

paragraphs: Keli cheres hamtzuppin ben otam habbaim meare yrvp" sheqqorin otam pirpuray (betzippuy abatz) ben otam hamtzuppin sheosin poh irenu, matbilam belo beraka "p shehem metzuppin mibbayit umichutz mishshum deikka pelugta bazeh vesapeq berakot lehaqel veim yesh lo keli acher shettaun beraka bevadday yatbilem immo beyachad kede shettoil habberaka gam leellu:

clarification.explanation: Glazed earthenware vessels (both those imported from Europe and those manufactured in Baghdad) are immersed without a blessing, since there is a dispute among the authorities whether they are obligated in immersion at all (out of doubt, no blessing is said — "a doubt in blessings is resolved leniently"). If one has another vessel certainly obligated in a blessing, it is worthwhile to immerse them together, so the blessing over the certain vessel also covers those in doubt.
takeaways: Glazed earthenware vessels are immersed without a blessing (out of doubt); it is worthwhile to immerse them together with a vessel certainly requiring a blessing, so the blessing covers both.

paragraphs: Meachar deikka pelugta bikle cheres hamtzuppin lekak chabiyyot gedolot shehem kele cheres metzuppin nahagu poh irenu shello lehatbilam kelal mishshum deikka tircha gedola bitbilatam veqasheh lehatbilam veayyen keneset haggedola uqehal yeuddeh umah shekkatab harab shulchan gabohha za"l behilkot pesach siman tn" sheyyittenem bemattana legoy veyishalem mimmennu ayyen sham lo nahagu bazeh poh irenu vehammachmir laasot kidbar harab za"l tabo alayv birkat tob;

clarification.explanation: Since there is a dispute regarding the law of glazed earthenware vessels, the custom in Baghdad was not to immerse large barrels that are glazed earthenware vessels at all, due to the great difficulty and effort involved in immersing them. What Rabbi "Shulchan Gavoah" wrote (regarding the laws of Passover) — that one may give them as a gift to a gentile and then borrow them back from him (thus avoiding immersion, since a borrowed vessel requires no immersion) — was not the Baghdad practice, but one who wishes to be stringent and follow his words is blessed.
takeaways: In Baghdad, large glazed earthenware barrels were not customarily immersed at all, due to the difficulty and the legal doubt.
One who wishes to be stringent may give them to a gentile as a gift and borrow them back.

paragraphs: Yeechoz hakkeli beripyon bishat tebila ulekattechilla yelachleach yadayv techilla beme hammiqveh atzmo veim kol zeh yizzaher shello yidchoq yadayv harbeh, vetzarik lehatbil gadol ben y"g shana veyom echad veen maaminim leqatan apillu al kele zekukkoyet ukele cheres metzuppin veayyen mishbetzot zahab orach chayyim siman tn".

clarification.explanation: During immersion, one should hold the vessel loosely (not tightly), and as the primary practice it is worthwhile to first moisten the hands with the mikveh's own water before holding it, but one must still be careful not to press too hard with the hands on the vessel (so the water reaches everywhere, including beneath the grip). The immersion must be performed by an adult (of bar-mitzvah age, thirteen years and a day) — a minor is not believed, even regarding glass vessels or glazed earthenware vessels (whose law is lighter).
takeaways: During immersion, hold the vessel loosely, and moisten the hands with the mikveh water beforehand.
The immersion must be performed by a bar-mitzvah-aged person, not a minor — even for lighter vessels.

paragraphs: Kelim shettashmishan lishpot alehem qedera kikli sheqqorin mntz"b (chatzuba) en taun tebila abal kelim sheddarkan litzlot alehem hammaakol atzmo teunin tebila vesakkin shel shechita veken sakkin shemmepatztzelim bah hattabbachim habbehema vesakkinim shemmeyuchadim lenaqqer bahem habbasar kol ellu yatbilem belo beraka abal sakkinim shechotekin bahem et happat o shear maakol veken hammazleg tzerikin tebila bibraka veken kissuy haqqedera matbil bibraka veken mashpek sheqqorin rycht"y vehabberazot matbil bibraka, abal harachat sheqqorin sy"k el msh"t (mardeh lirdot lechem mittannur) yatbil belo beraka veayyen peri chadash seip qatan t"v:

clarification.explanation: Vessels whose function is only to support a pot (such as a trivet) require no immersion at all, since they have no direct contact with the food. But vessels on which the food itself is normally roasted (such as a roasting grate) do require immersion. A slaughtering knife, a knife for cutting up the animal, and knives specially designated for trimming meat — all these are immersed without a blessing. But knives for cutting bread or other food, and likewise a fork, are obligated in immersion with a blessing. A pot lid, a funnel, and a faucet are also immersed with a blessing. But a peel (a tool for removing bread from the oven) is immersed without a blessing.
takeaways: Vessels merely supporting a pot (a trivet) are exempt from immersion; slaughtering/trimming knives are immersed without a blessing; eating knives, forks, pot lids, funnels, and faucets are immersed with a blessing; a bread peel is immersed without a blessing.

paragraphs: Dod gadol shemmartichin bo hattemad lehotzi mehem shekar veken david sheqqorin lmby"q (david leziquq kohal) shemmelakto gam ken kak yatbil belo beraka ak lepi gadelam qasheh lehatbil otam al ken yittenennu legoy bemattana veyachazor veyishalennu mimmennu ukemo shekkatab hashshulchan gabohha gabbe chabiyyot gedolot veayyen pachad yitzchaq maareket haelep dap n"g veayyen shiyyure beraka ot z' veerek hashshulchan ot y" mihu hakkeli sheyyored bo hashshekar sheqqorin bearbe pr"g (mikal leqibbul hakkohal min hamtaqqen leziqquq) yatbil bibraka uqedera gedola kemo dud shemmeyuchedet lechammem bah mayim bishbil hakkebisa en tzerika tebila v"p shellipamim kesheyyihyeh chuppa o mila verotzim lechalleq laaniyyim tabshil harbeh mebashshelim bah en holekin bikli ella achar rob tashmisho veayyen peri chadash seip qatan y"b vy"t veshulchan gabohha yoreh dea siman q"k seip qatan t"z uqedera gedola shemmagilim bah kelim letzorek chag happesach yesh omerim shetztzerika tebila veyesh omerim enah tzerika, lekak yatbilenna belo beraka veayyen erek hashshulchan:

clarification.explanation: A large boiler in which "tamad" (a beverage) is boiled to produce beer, and likewise an "alembic" (a distillation vessel) — require immersion, but should be immersed without a blessing; and since it is difficult to immerse them due to their size, one should give them to a gentile as a gift and then borrow them back (Shulchan Gavoah, regarding large barrels). But the vessel into which the beer/spirits descend ("farag") should be immersed with a blessing. A large pot designated for heating laundry water requires no immersion, and even though sometimes a large quantity of food is cooked in it for charitable distribution to the poor, one follows the vessel's predominant use. A large pot used to purge vessels for Passover — some say it requires immersion and some say it does not, so it should be immersed without a blessing.
takeaways: Large beer/spirits-production vessels require immersion without a blessing, and due to their size should be given to a gentile as a gift and borrowed back.
The vessel receiving the finished beverage ("farag") is immersed with a blessing; a laundry-water pot is exempt (follows predominant use).
A pot used to purge Passover vessels — a doubt, immersed without a blessing.

paragraphs: Shepud shetztzolin bo yatbilennu bibraka veken keli sheshshoabin bo mayim lishtiyya yatbil bibraka veayyen chakemat adam yoreh dea, medoka shel barzel ushear mattakot veken hayyad shel hamdoka yatbil bibraka abal medoka hamyuchedet laduk bah haggarinim shel hqhvv" (qph) bilbad veen dakim bah debarim acherim shel maakol yatbil belo beraka veharechayim shel mine mattakot shettochanin bah pilpelin matbilan bibraka abal harechayim shettochanin bah qhvv bilbad yatbil belo beraka veayyen mishbetzot zahab orach chayyim siman tn" s"q v' upitche teshuba seip qatan ch vechakemat adam vehakkeli sheqqorin rlyy"v (migreret pumpiyya) sheggorerin bo haggebina shehu lucha barzel naqub kikbara qabua bemasmerin al dap etz tzarik tebila bibraka ki habbarzel hu haiqqar kemo shekkatab hashshulchan gabohha za"l behilkot pesach siman tn":

clarification.explanation: A roasting skewer — immersion with a blessing. A vessel for drawing drinking water — immersion with a blessing. A mortar (a pounding vessel) of iron or other metal, and likewise its pestle — immersion with a blessing. But a mortar designated only for pounding coffee beans (not other foods) — immersion without a blessing. A metal mill for grinding pepper — immersion with a blessing, but a mill designated only for grinding coffee — immersion without a blessing. A cheese grater made of a perforated iron plate attached to wood — immersion with a blessing, since the iron is its primary component.
takeaways: A skewer, a water-drawing vessel, a general metal mortar, and a pepper mill — immersion with a blessing.
A mortar/mill designated only for coffee — immersion without a blessing; a cheese grater (primarily iron) — immersion with a blessing.

paragraphs: Kele mattakot shellashin bahem haissa veken kele mattakot sheorekin alehem hammatztzot letzorek chag hammatztzot yatbilem belo beraka veayyen bet yeuddeh siman n"v:

clarification.explanation: Metal vessels used for kneading dough, and likewise metal vessels on which matzot are rolled out for Passover, are immersed without a blessing.
takeaways: Metal vessels for kneading dough and rolling matzot are immersed without a blessing.

paragraphs: Kele eben ukele etz en teunin tebila veillu im qabua barzel dei epshar lehishtammesh bahem belo habbarzel en taun tebila ukele etz sheyyesh lo chishshuqim shel barzel mibbachutz shemmaamidim oto yesh omerim taun tebila veyesh omerim en taun tebila lekak yatbilennu belo beraka veshulchan shel etz shemmechubbar "y chishshuqe barzel en tzarik tebila mippene d"g demannichin hallechem al hashshulchan atzmo belo biqara mikkol maqom darkam lipros mappa al hashshulchan veim lipamim mannichim belo mappa en holekim bikli ella achar rob tashmisho vaapillu im nomar hammappa betela legabbe hashshulchan ukeillu lekka mappa mikkol maqom haddap shel hashshulchan shemmannichim alayv hammaakol yakol lehishtammesh bo lebaddo vehachashuqim baim lachabero baregalim kede lehagbiho venimtza habbarzel tashmish detashmish:

clarification.explanation: Stone and wood vessels require no immersion. And if iron is fixed into them such that they cannot be used without it, they still require no immersion. A wood vessel with external iron hoops holding it together — some say it requires immersion and some say it does not, so it should be immersed without a blessing. A wood table joined with iron hoops requires no immersion: even though bread is sometimes placed directly on the table without a plate, the custom is to spread a cloth over it; and if sometimes without a cloth, one follows the predominant use; and even if one were to say the cloth is nullified relative to the table, the board on which the food is placed can function alone, with the hoops serving only to join it to the legs and raise it, so the iron is "a utensil for a utensil" (serving what serves).
takeaways: Stone and wood vessels are exempt from immersion, even with indispensable fixed iron.
A wood vessel with external iron hoops is a doubt, immersed without a blessing.
A wood table with iron hoops is exempt, since the iron is "a utensil for a utensil" (only joining and raising it).

paragraphs: Im nipchat shule hakkeli debatel bekol tashmish veasa lo haggoy shulayim mattas chadash tzarik atta lehatbilo bibraka kemo keli shekkullo chadash ukeli cheres hamtzuppeh shennishbar lishnayim vedibbeqo haggoy bedebeq matbilo belo beraka veayyen eshel abraham orach chayyim sop siman tn" ukele mattakot shel yisrael shemmetzuppim otam bibdil "y goy en tzerikin tebila dehatztzippuy shel bedil la have maamid ubatel hu legabbe haggalle vekatab happeri chadash shekken hamminhag pashut ayyen sham veken hamminhag poh irenu bagdad veap al gab demishbetzot zahab beorach chayyim veken bet lechem yeuddeh sebira lehu deyatbilem belo beraka lo nahagu haolam bekak:

clarification.explanation: If a vessel's bottom broke through (so the vessel is entirely unusable), and a gentile fitted it with a new metal bottom, it must now be immersed with a blessing, exactly like an entirely new vessel. But a glazed earthenware vessel broken in two, which a gentile glued back together, is immersed without a blessing (since no truly new vessel was made). A Jew's metal vessels that a gentile coated with tin require no additional immersion, since the tin coating does not "establish" the vessel (is not essential to its function) and is secondary and subordinate to the original vessel — so ruled the "Peri Chadash," and this is the accepted custom, including in Baghdad, although some disagree (holding at least immersion without a blessing).
takeaways: A vessel with an entirely broken bottom replaced by a new metal one requires immersion with a blessing, like a new vessel; a glued (not replaced) glazed vessel — immersion without a blessing.
A metal vessel merely tin-coated by a gentile requires no additional immersion, since the coating is subordinate to the original vessel.

paragraphs: Yisrael sheqqana kelim lischora asur lehishtammesh bahem apillu aray belo tebila abal im yisrael acher shaal kelim ellu mimmennu muttar lehishtammesh bahem belo tebila dehammashil lo qenaam letzarekko ella qenaam lischora veyesh choleqin usebira lehu detzarik lehatbil veken rauy lehorot veraq im hem kele zekukit o kelim hamtzuvvim sheqqorin prpvr"y (cheres betzippuy matteket) yesh lismok al hammeqillin bishat haddechaq bilbad veayyen binat adam upitche teshuba vehaynu davqa im hitna immo sheim yishshaberu yeshallem lo deme haqqeren shellahem davqa abal im hitna sheyyeshallem kepi haerek shehu marvicha az gam bishat haddechaq en lismok al hammeqillin ki zeh chashib miqqach velo sheela ukemo shekkatab chinnuk bet yeuddeh siman n"b vehebio pitche teshuba.

clarification.explanation: A Jew who bought vessels for business purposes (for resale) may not use them even temporarily without immersion. But if another Jew borrows these vessels from him, he may use them without immersion, since the lender did not buy them for himself but for resale, and they are therefore not considered an "acquisition" for personal use. Some disagree and hold that even the borrower is obligated in immersion — and this is the proper practical ruling. Only for glass vessels or glazed earthenware vessels (which are common) may one rely on the lenient view in a pressing situation only — and only if the agreement was that if the vessels break, he will pay their principal value (not according to the profit he would have made from selling them), since otherwise the loan is considered a sale rather than a loan.
takeaways: Vessels bought for business require immersion even for temporary use; one who merely borrows them (not buys) — the proper ruling is that he too is obligated, though glass/glazed earthenware allow leniency in a pressing situation.
The leniency depends on the agreement being principal-value payment for breakage, not profit-based — otherwise it is considered a sale, not a loan.

paragraphs: Yisrael shennatan kesep leumman goy laasot lo mimmennu keli eno tzarik tebila vezehu daat mera"n za"l abal rama" za"l sebira lehu lehatbilo belo beraka veken rauy lehorot. veim yisrael natan leyisrael kesep bishlichut haggoy laasot keli legoy venimlak uleqacho yisrael leatzmo en tzarik tebila deha lo ba lirshut haggoy veen shelichut legoy veayyen peri toar seip qatan y"d:

clarification.explanation: A Jew who gave money to a gentile craftsman to make him a vessel from that money — the vessel requires no immersion, since according to Maran the vessel was never in the gentile's ownership at all (he only built it for the Jew for a fee). The Rema disagrees and holds it should be immersed without a blessing — and this is the proper practical ruling. If a Jew gave money to another Jew as an agent on behalf of a gentile (to make a vessel for the gentile), and in the end the agent changed his mind and took the vessel for himself — no immersion is needed at all, since the vessel never actually reached the gentile's domain (there is no "agency for a gentile" — that is, the act is not attributed to him).
takeaways: A vessel commissioned from a gentile craftsman with a Jew's money (not bought ready-made) — by Maran's view exempt from immersion, but in practice immersed without a blessing, following the Rema.
A vessel commissioned for a gentile but never actually reaching his possession is entirely exempt from immersion.

paragraphs: Tzarik lenaqqot hakkeli mikkol likluk vachaludda shello yihyeh chatzitza vetzarik sheyyabou hammayim al hakkeli ben mibbipnim ben mibbachutz veim hitbilo derek piv en hammayim niknasim beshulayv ukeillu lo tabal veharotzeh lehatbil keli sheppiv tzar yemalleennu mayim veyatbilennu, ukeli shel issur shetztzarik lo heksher "y libbun o hagala yakshirennu techilla vech"k yatbilennu veim hitbilo qodem heksher yesh pelugta bah lekak yachazor veyatbilennu achar heksher belo beraka .

clarification.explanation: Before immersion, the vessel must be cleaned of all dirt and rust, so there is no "chatzitzah" (an interposing substance between the water and the vessel). The water must reach every part of the vessel, both inside and outside — and if it was immersed only through its opening and the water did not reach the bottom (due to its shape), it is as though it was not immersed at all. One who wishes to immerse a vessel with a narrow opening should first fill it with water and then immerse it (so the water inside already touches the bottom). A vessel containing a forbidden substance (a forbidden taste) requiring koshering by fire-scorching or purging must first be koshered, and only then immersed. If it was immersed before koshering, there is a dispute whether the immersion is effective, and therefore it must be immersed again after koshering, without a blessing.
takeaways: The vessel must be thoroughly cleaned of dirt and rust (interposing substances) before immersion, and water must reach every part — a narrow-mouthed vessel should be filled with water first.
A vessel requiring koshering (fire-scorching/purging) must be koshered first; if immersed beforehand, it must be immersed again afterward, without a blessing.

paragraphs: Im nishtammesh bikli hatztzarik tebila qodem shehitbilo en neesar hammaakol vetzarik lehatbilo apillu nishtammesh bo kamma peamim:

clarification.explanation: If a vessel obligated in immersion was used before being immersed, the food prepared in it is not forbidden, but the vessel itself still requires immersion — even if it was already used several times beforehand.
takeaways: Using a vessel before its immersion does not forbid the food, but the vessel itself remains obligated in immersion, even after repeated use.
